title: Shared Credentialing: Still Leaving You With the Hardest Part?
summary: Shared credentialing promises lower costs, but NCQA timelines, state clocks, and plan policies leave work on your plate. Questions to ask before you commit.
body_markdown:
*Jocelyne, a healthcare executive with 20 years of leadership experience, consults for Verifiable.*


‍


‍


Every health plan credentialing the same provider, separately, from a blank file, is wasteful. Nobody seriously disagrees. So when CertifyOS's SharedCred and Medallion's CredAlliance arrived promising shared verification across participating plans, executives heard "shared cost" and started drafting the press release.


‍


On a whiteboard, it's gorgeous. Whiteboards, of course, don’t face[delegated credentialing](https://verifiable.com/blog/delegated-credentialing-getting-providers-seeing-patients-faster-reimbursed-sooner) audits.


‍


On paper, the model makes a lot of sense. The open question is how comfortably it fits every plan’s committee process and regulatory obligations. Let’s look at what health plans should be considering and questions they should be asking when evaluating a shared credentialing model.


‍


## **What is driving health plans to consider a shared credentialing model in the first place?**


The pressure to lower costs is a dominant force in how health plans make decisions today. When reimbursements can't rise, executives are under pressure to take out administrative costs, and when they hear "shared credentialing," they tend to hear "shared cost."


‍


Provider abrasion is also a consideration. Providers have to re-engage, respond, and re-attest. In theory, a shared model would let a provider complete one application to enroll with multiple health plans, reducing their burden.


‍


At face value it seems like a shared credentialing model is a great way to deal with these downsides to doing credentialing “the old way”, but will the results be consistent with promises made by shared credentialing vendors? We’ve seen multiple vendors promote the model, but have yet to see enough momentum to make it successful. Let’s look at some hurdles that make the model difficult to execute and truly see benefit from.


‍


### 1. The clock starts before you do.


NCQA limits how old[primary source verification](https://verifiable.com/blog/ncqa-primary-source-verification-requirements) results can be when they're used for credentialing, with timeframes that vary by verification element and accreditation or certification program. Under its current credentialing framework, some elements have a 120-day window, others 180 days, and CVO certification has its own requirements.


‍


A packet verified for the group is already aging when it reaches you, and your committee meets on your schedule, not the pool's. When a[verification ages](https://verifiable.com/provider-network-monitoring) out, somebody has to pull it again. You didn't get a head start. You got a shorter runway.


‍


### 2. "Verify once" has an asterisk the size of a federal database.


A packet built to[NCQA standards](https://verifiable.com/resources/ncqa-guidelines-ebook) and an agreed-upon set of additional requirements can still miss a plan whose policy goes further. Shared credentialing vendors sometimes offer add-ons on top of the shared packet, which can get you to your final goal, but expect to pay extra for these. This should be factored in when you’re evaluating whether the shared model will truly reduce costs.


‍


Even in SharedCred's own model, restricted sources like the NPDB stay under each plan's control and aren't pooled, so that requirement doesn't disappear. Every plan also keeps its own policies, committee and decisions, which is the point of being its own plan.


‍


Verifiable's Director of Credentialing, Courtney Ivess, has seen how this goes. At a previous organization, she tried to get markets under one roof to accept each other's credentialing decisions. One approved nearly everyone at committee. Another had strict board certification rules. Neither would accept the other's decisions.


‍


If two markets under one roof can't share a decision, I'd love to watch competing plans try.


‍


### 3. States don't care about the vendor's roadmap.


Plans get audited against applicable state requirements, not shared credentialing metrics. Rhode Island requires covered plans to make credentialing decisions within 45 calendar days of receiving a complete application and to notify applicants within five business days once their application is complete. North Carolina requires insurers to maintain a credentialing process within 60 days of receiving a complete application, with specific provisions for temporary credentials when that deadline isn't met.


‍


Your regulator will not accept "the pool was running late" as a corrective action plan. Verifiable's SVP of Operations, Janan Dave, puts it plainly, “Until states and payers align on requirements, the pain doesn't go away, it just moves to the payer's side.”


‍


The vendors say they handle date alignment and plan-specific rules, but I have my doubts. What happens when a verification ages out before your decision date, or a state clock is shorter than the group's?


‍


### 4. Overlap is not duplication, and the vendor's own footnote says so.


SharedCred's page cites a JAMA Network Open study, built on 2019 directory data, finding that roughly 57% of primary-care providers and 62% of cardiology providers are shared between competing networks, on average.


‍


Then it adds a footnote: those figures measure provider participation overlap, not credentialing duplication.


‍


Their words, not mine.


‍


Providers sitting in many networks tells you nothing by itself about how much of your credentialing work is actually duplicated, or how much a shared packet can touch.


Run your own numbers before you borrow theirs.


‍


### 5. Provider abrasion is just moved, not eliminated


In theory, a single application for a provider to join multiple health plan networks seems like the dream, but just because credentialing is being handled by the same vendor doesn’t mean the entire process is dealt with via that vendor. Does your health plan still require providers to follow a secondary application process that is not covered by the shared model?


‍


When you look under the hood (or past the whiteboard) of a shared credentialing model and start asking these questions, it doesn’t seem so simple after all. The model is too new for any vendor to really prove that it’s effective in reducing costs and friction, while maintaining quality and turnaround time.


‍


## What factors should you consider when looking at a credentialing vendor, whether a shared model or not?


A compliant packet, cheap and fast, with as little left on your plate as possible. Ask any model these questions:


- Does it produce a packet compliant with NCQA, state rules, and my own policies?
- Does turnaround depend on other plans' workflows?
- Who sets the shared requirements and timelines, and do I get a vote?
- How many plan-level credentialing events remain after the packet arrives?
- How much do I have to pay for add-ons to the shared packet?
- If I join and it doesn’t deliver what was promised, what does leaving cost me?


‍


## Where Verifiable brings value and reduces cost, without forcing you to share


Verifiable deliberately doesn’t run a shared model, because verification isn’t where the cost lives. The automation technology runs against[3,500+ direct sources](https://verifiable.com/primary-source-verification) at a 99% success rate. Building the packet, flagging exceptions, and routing files to committee round out the end-to-end process. Enabled by automation, each specialist can handle up to 10x the volume, and packet costs drop up to 90% - no sharing required.


‍


NCQA is the floor, not the ceiling. About 80% of the steps are custom to each organization: state clocks, plan policies, and committee documentation. That work is built in, not sold as an add-on. Clean packets from Verifiable’s NCQA-certified CVO average 1.3 days, and turnaround is a contractual SLA.


‍


## Compare before you commit


Sharing a packet doesn't share the accountability. When the audit comes, it's your name on the file, your state's clock, and your committee's decision. The question was never whether verification could be shared. The question is who handles everything that comes after it. Before you commit, compare side by side what a shared model leaves on your plate and what Verifiable takes off.
